interactions.summary: Jiang closes the prior example by saying religion and material interest are often hard to separate in practice.
The host asks whether analysis becomes harder in an allegedly secular capitalist age where religion and community seem weakened.

Jiang rejects the secularization premise, arguing that religion has only been reinterpreted into forms like science and capitalism, with money and central banking functioning as priestly belief systems.
The host pushes back that money has real coercive force because survival and punishment are materially organized through it, even if its value is imagined.
Jiang concedes money has social force through use while insisting that, from first principles, it lacks intrinsic value and is wrongly treated by economists as self-grounding.

speaker_notes.note: The line transcribed as 'sad analyses' is likely ASR damage for 'such analyses' or 'that analysis,' but the question's secularization pressure is clear.
There is heavy ASR damage in Jiang's attack on science, including references to validation and string theory, so only the stable argumentative spine is extracted.

claims.claim: Jiang says analysts wrongly oppose secularity and religion because modern societies remain religious even when belief is reinterpreted rather than openly confessed.
Jiang argues that science and capitalism function as religions rather than neutral secular domains.
Jiang says money is an imaginative belief structure whose reality depends on collective faith, which is why central bankers operate like a new high-priest class.
Jiang argues that labeling modern doctrine as secular gives it extra authority by pretending it comes from scientific first principles rather than from faith commitments.
Jiang says the prestige of science depends partly on mystery and priestly mediation, because a fully transparent science would lose some of its authority.
The host argues that money becomes materially real because social life, basic survival, and state coercion are organized through it.
Jiang partially agrees that use gives money force but insists it has no intrinsic value by itself and that economists mistake socially sustained value for inherent value.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang recasts central bankers as a new priesthood whose sacred power depends on belief in money.
signature_moments.source_phrase: central bankers almost as a new high priest class
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is one of the most memorable images in the interview and compresses his religion-under-capitalism argument into one reusable figure.

signature_moments.moment: He provokes by saying science keeps authority partly because mystery and sacred distance have not really disappeared.
signature_moments.source_phrase: if science was completely knowable as it purports to be then it loses its power
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is a direct reversal of the common secular story and shows how he folds science back into the category of religion.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The host proposes it as a modern condition; Jiang rejects the label and treats modern secularity as disguised religion.
Jiang uses this for central bankers and, more broadly, elite interpreters who sustain belief in the monetary order.
The host and Jiang use it to distinguish money's coercive social force from any self-grounding value in the object itself.

chronology_notes.note: This interview records Jiang making an explicit 2025-era argument that science and capitalism should be read as religions rather than as post-religious secular systems.

uncertainty_notes.note: The packet contains significant ASR noise around Jiang's criticism of scientific validation and physics, so the extraction avoids over-precise claims about the specific scientific examples.
